body_markdown:
An OSHA compliance officer walks your shop floor and asks to see three things: last year's noise survey, the baseline hearing test for the welder you hired in March, and the letter you sent the forklift driver whose hearing changed. You've kept foam earplugs stocked at every station for years. But you can’t find the records you need.


A hearing conservation program is the set of noise monitoring, hearing testing, protection, training, and recordkeeping duties that OSHA requires under[29 CFR 1910.95(c)](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.95) once an employee's noise exposure reaches an 8-hour average of 85 decibels. Stocked earplugs cover one of those duties. The records are how you show an inspector that the rest of the program happened too.


General industry employers work under 29 CFR 1910.95, and construction contractors work under a shorter rule,[1926.52](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.52) .


This guide is general information and not legal advice, so confirm your obligations with your safety professional or[OSHA's free On-Site Consultation Program](https://www.osha.gov/consultation) .


## Does Your Workplace Need a Hearing Conservation Program?


Your workplace needs a hearing conservation program if any employee's noise exposure equals or exceeds an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) of 85 decibels.[Under 1910.95(c)(1)](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.95) , that exposure requires a "continuing, effective hearing conservation program." OSHA calls 85 dBA the action level, measured on the A scale with a slow meter response.


OSHA measures the noise in the air, not the protection in your ears. A crew that already wears earplugs or earmuffs still counts, because the exposure calculation gives no credit for hearing protection. NIOSH estimates that[about 22 million U.S. workers are exposed to hazardous noise each year](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2022/noise-50.html) .


OSHA's[noise in construction guide](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/3498NOISE-IN-CONSTRUCTION-POCKET-GUIDE.pdf) says that if you have to raise your voice to be heard 2 to 3 feet away, you should assume the sound level is at or above 85 dBA.


### Your Workplace Has More Duties Above 90 dBA


The 85 dBA action level starts the program, and the 90 dBA permissible exposure limit (PEL) in 1910.95(b) adds to it. Above the PEL, you also need feasible engineering or administrative controls. Our[guide to OSHA hearing protection requirements](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/osha-hearing-protection-requirements-what-employers-and-workers-need-to-know) covers the PEL, the 5 dB exchange rate and Table G-16.


### Construction, Oil and Gas, and State Plan Workplaces Follow Different Rules


On a construction site, 1926.52(d)(1) requires "a continuing, effective hearing conservation program" wherever sound levels exceed the Table D-2 limits, which start at 90 dBA for an 8-hour day. Because 1926.52 doesn't list program elements, many contractors use the 1910.95 steps as a template, ideally confirmed with a safety professional. Our[guide to hearing protection for construction](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/hearing-protection-for-construction) covers jobsite specifics.


1910.95(o) exempts oil and gas well drilling and servicing from paragraphs (c) through (n), and State Plan states can set stricter rules.


If your workplace crosses the 85 dBA action level, every requirement that follows has its own deadline and its own record.


## OSHA Hearing Conservation Program Requirements in One Table


Once a workplace reaches the 85 dBA action level, OSHA's requirements cover 10 duties in 1910.95(c) through (m), plus the OSHA 300 log rule in 1904.10. You can print this table and use it as your audit sheet.


Step Requirement What you must do Deadline Record


1 Monitoring, 1910.95(d) Measure anyone who may reach 85 dBA TWA At the start and after process or equipment changes Exposure measurements


1 Notification, (e) Share results with employees at or above 85 dBA After each round Copy of notice


1 Observation, (f) Let employees watch monitoring Each round None specified


2 Audiometric testing, (g) Offer free baseline and annual tests Baseline within 6 months, then yearly Audiograms


3 STS follow-up, (g)(7) to (g)(8) Notify, refit or retrain, refer Notice within 21 days STS notice


4 Hearing protectors, (i) Offer a free variety, fit and supervise Ongoing Issue records


4 Attenuation, (j) Confirm 90 dBA or below (85 after an STS) When choosing protectors Evaluation worksheet


5 Training, (k) Cover three required topics Yearly Attendance


6 Access, (l) Post the standard, share OSHA materials Ongoing Posted standard


6 Recordkeeping, (m) Keep and share records Exposure 2 years; audiograms for employment Records


7 300 log, 1904.10 Record qualifying STS cases 7 calendar days 300 log entry


You'll often see the program reduced to five elements: monitoring, audiometric testing, hearing protectors, training, and recordkeeping. An inspector can also ask about notification, attenuation evaluation, and access to information, so keep all three in your audit.


Noise monitoring, the first row in the table, produces the data every other requirement depends on, including which hearing protectors you can issue.


## Step 1: Measure Noise Before You Buy Hearing Protection


Noise monitoring tells you who needs hearing protection and how much protection each worker needs, so measure before you order earplugs or earmuffs.


Under 1910.95(d)(1), you must monitor when any employee may reach 85 dBA TWA. 1910.95(d)(1)(i) says your sampling strategy must identify program members and "enable the proper selection of hearing protectors."


Without a measured TWA, you can't run the 1910.95(j) attenuation check on any Noise Reduction Rating (NRR).


### Choose Personal Dosimetry or Area Sampling


1910.95(d)(1)(ii) requires personal dosimetry, a meter worn all day, where workers move around, levels vary, or impulse noise is significant, unless area sampling gives you equivalent results.


### Set Your Dosimeter to Capture Sound From 80 dB


1910.95(d)(2)(i) requires all sound from 80 to 130 decibels in the measurement. A dosimeter that ignores sound below 85 or 90 dB, instead of 80, can undercount a worker's dose and lead you to choose hearing protectors with inadequate protection.


### Measure Again When Equipment or Processes Change


1910.95(d)(3) requires new monitoring when a change in process, equipment, or controls could add employees at 85 dBA or make your current hearing protectors inadequate. Under (e) and (f), you share the results with those employees and let them observe the measurements.


Our[guide to what decibel level requires ear protection](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/what-db-level-requires-ear-protection-a-complete-decibel-guide) lists what common tools measure, and can help you decide where to start monitoring.


Everyone your monitoring places at or above 85 dBA TWA also needs a hearing test, timed from their first day of workplace noise exposure.


## Step 2: Baseline and Annual Hearing Tests


Every employee at or above 85 dBA TWA needs a baseline audiogram, then an annual audiogram compared against that baseline. Under 1910.95(g)(1) and (g)(2), these tests come at no cost to the employee. Under (g)(3), an audiologist, otolaryngologist, physician, or qualified technician can give the tests.


### Baseline and Annual Hearing Test Deadlines


Under (g)(5)(i), the baseline test is due within 6 months of an employee’s first workplace noise exposure, after 14 hours without workplace noise, or with protectors worn.


A mobile test van gets 1 year under (g)(5)(ii), with protectors required after month 6. Under (g)(6), annual audiograms follow at least once a year. Under (g)(5)(iv), tell employees to avoid loud non-work noise, like shooting, in those 14 hours.


**Tip:** Schedule the baseline hearing test during onboarding for new hires in noisy roles, since new hires are the easiest baselines to miss.


### What Each Hearing Test Includes


Under 1910.95(h), each test is a pure tone, air conduction exam at 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, and 6000 Hz, one ear at a time. Confirm the calibration and Appendix D test room standards in your provider contract.


Three of those frequencies, 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz, are the numbers you'll use to calculate whether a worker's hearing has changed.


## Step 3: How to Calculate a Standard Threshold Shift


You calculate a standard threshold shift (STS) by comparing each ear's annual audiogram to its baseline at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz. Under 1910.95(g)(10)(i), an average change of 10 dB or more in either ear is an STS, and under (g)(7)(i) a technician can do the comparison.


### Calculate the STS in Three Steps


1. Pull the baseline and annual hearing levels at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz for one ear.
2. Subtract the baseline level from the annual level at each frequency.
3. Average the three changes. A result of 10 dB or more is an STS. Repeat for the other ear.


### Age Correction Can Change the Result


Under (g)(10)(ii), Appendix F lets you correct the annual audiogram for age, which can bring a borderline result under 10 dB. Ask your testing provider to apply the age correction before you treat a result as final.


### Act Within 21 Days When the Calculation Shows an STS


1. Retest within 30 days if you choose to, and treat the retest as the annual audiogram ((g)(7)(ii)).
2. Notify the employee in writing within 21 days ((g)(8)(i)).
3. Fit and train an employee who wasn't using hearing protectors and require their use, or refit and retrain one who was, with more protection if needed ((g)(8)(ii)(A) and (B)).
4. Refer for a clinical audiological or otological exam where appropriate ((g)(8)(ii)(C)).
5. From then on, that employee's protectors must bring exposure to 85 dBA TWA or below ((j)(3)).


These steps apply unless a physician finds the STS isn't work-related, and most of the steps involve fitting or upgrading a hearing protector. That work goes faster when your program already offers several protectors to choose from.


## Step 4: Offer a Variety of Suitable Hearing Protectors


Under 1910.95(i)(3), employees must be able to choose from "a variety of suitable hearing protectors" that you provide as an employer. Under (i)(1), protectors should come at no cost to employees, and under (i)(2) they're mandatory above the 90 dBA PEL, after 6 months without a baseline, and after an STS.


### What a Variety of Suitable Hearing Protectors Includes


- [Foam or silicone earplugs](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/silicone-vs-foam-earplugs) for general use
- [A reusable or valved earplug](https://goaxil.com/pages/x-series-earplugs) for workers who switch between noisy and less noisy tasks
- [Earmuffs](https://goaxil.com/collections/ear-muffs) for workers who take protection on and off often
- [Electronic earbuds](https://goaxil.com/collections/ear-buds) or[electronic earmuffs](https://goaxil.com/collections/ear-muffs) for roles that need to hear coworkers, radios or backup alarms


Our[guide to earplugs for work](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/what-makes-the-best-earplugs-for-work) compares comfort for full-day wear, and under (i)(4) and (i)(5) you have to fit and train employees on every option. Consumer earbuds and noise-cancelling headphones without a published NRR don't count. Our[explainer on why noise cancellation is not hearing protection](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/cancellation-vs-protection) covers the difference.


### Every Option Has to Pass the Appendix B Check


Under 1910.95(j)(1), you evaluate each protector's attenuation for its noise environment using[Appendix B](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.95AppB) , which calls the NRR on the package the most convenient method. You can read about how NRR is measured in[our NRR guide](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/nrr-rating-for-shooting-everything-you-need-to-know-axil) , and[AXIL's ANSI test reports list each of our products’ rating](https://goaxil.com/pages/axil-certifications) s.


With A-weighted TWA data, subtract 7 dB from the NRR, then subtract that result from the TWA.


[AXIL's GS Extreme 3.0](https://goaxil.com/products/gs-extreme-3-0) is rated 21 dB NRR with foam tips and 17 dB NRR with silicone tips, so the tip a worker picks changes the result. Worked example: at a 95 dBA TWA, foam tips give an estimated 95 - (21 - 7) = 81 dBA under the protector, while silicone tips give 95 - (17 - 7) = 85 dBA.


**Tip:** Record the tip type with the model number when you issue electronic earbuds for your workers.


### The 7 dB Rule and the 50 Percent Factor Answer Different Questions


[OSHA notes that it subtracts only 7 dB when judging protector adequacy, and applies an additional 50 percent safety factor only when weighing whether the employer should implement engineering controls](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2016-04-29) . For very high exposures, see[our guide to doubling up with plugs and muffs](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/doubling-up-with-plugs-and-muffs) .


Once you've chosen the ear protectors your program will offer, annual training is where your employees learn to choose and wear each one.


## Step 5: What Hearing Conservation Training Must Cover


Under 1910.95(k)(3), hearing conservation training must cover three topics:


1. The effects of noise on hearing
2. The purpose of hearing protectors, the advantages, disadvantages, and attenuation of various types, and instructions on selection, fitting, use, and care for the equipment
3. The purpose of audiometric testing and an explanation of the test procedures


The second topic is where your employees learn how each protector in your variety differs.


### Who Attends, How Often and What to Add


Under (k)(1) and (k)(2), annual hearing conservation education is required for every employee exposed at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 decibels. As good practice, run a hands-on fit check and document attendance, since OSHA can request training materials under (l)(3).


### A Five-Minute Toolbox Talk That Covers All Three Topics


1. Name today's noise sources, and explain that noise damage builds up and hearing levels don’t come back.
2. Have everyone insert their earplugs or fit their earmuffs, and check each seal.
3. Remind the crew that hearing protectors work only while they're in, and specify who they can approach if they need a different hearing protector.
4. Tell the crew when annual hearing tests are scheduled and what the test involves.


Attendance sheets from these sessions belong with your program records, which have their own set of rules.


## Step 6: Hearing Conservation Recordkeeping Requirements


OSHA's recordkeeping requirements under 1910.95(m) cover noise exposure measurements, audiometric test records, and test room background sound levels.


### What Each Audiometric Record Must Include


Under (m)(2), each audiometric record lists the employee's name and job classification, the audiogram date, the examiner's name, the audiometer's last acoustic or exhaustive calibration date, and the employee's most recent noise exposure assessment.


### How Long to Keep Records and Who Can See Them


Under (m)(3), you must keep noise exposure measurements for 2 years and audiometric test records for the duration of the employee's employment. 29 CFR 1910.1020 can require longer retention for some records, so confirm this with your safety professional.


Under (m)(4), records must be available on request to employees, former employees, their representatives, and OSHA, and under (m)(5) they must be transferred to a successor employer. Under 1910.95(l), you must also post the noise standard and share OSHA's materials.


One more record sits outside 1910.95. A hearing loss case that meets two tests also goes on your OSHA 300 log.


## Step 7: Recording Hearing Loss Cases on the 300 Log


Under 29 CFR 1904.10, a hearing loss case goes on your OSHA 300 log only when the case meets two tests: the shift has to be work-related, and the ear's hearing level has to average 25 dB or more above audiometric zero. Then check the log's hearing loss column once you've confirmed both.


### Two Tests Decide Whether a Case Is Recordable


Under 1904.10(a), the same ear must show a work-related STS and a total hearing level of 25 dB or more above audiometric zero, averaged at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz.


### Retests, Age Adjustments, and Work-Relatedness


Under 1904.10(b)(3), age adjustment applies to the STS check but not the 25 dB check. Under (b)(4), a 30-day retest that doesn't confirm the STS means no entry, and a confirmed case should be recorded within seven calendar days.


Work-relatedness follows 1904.5, and a physician or licensed health care professional can determine that a loss isn't work-related.


A recordable case means a worker has already lost some hearing. The checks below are how you catch program gaps before a case like that reaches your 300 log.


## What Makes a Hearing Conservation Program Effective


1910.95(c)(1) asks for a "continuing, effective" program. OSHA describes these programs as working to prevent initial occupational hearing loss and preserve remaining hearing. These annual checks show whether your program is doing what 1910.95(c)(1) asks for:


- Monitoring is repeated after every equipment or process change.
- A baseline test is conducted for every new hire within 6 months.
- Employees get a choice of more than one earplug model, since one size won't seal in every ear.
- Training includes a hands-on fit check.
- STS letters go out within 21 days, followed by a protection change.
- Hearing protectors stay in when workers need to hear coworkers, radios or alarms.


Time with earplugs out still counts toward a worker's noise dose, which makes that last check the hardest to pass.


### Effective Programs Require Ear Protectors for Roles That Need Communication


Electronic hearing protection amplifies low-level sounds, such as speech and alarms, and compresses loud sounds to a safer level to protect an employee’s ear. AXIL calls this[Protect + Enhance](https://goaxil.com/) . For a forklift spotter or a crew lead on a radio, that circuit can remove the main reason people pull their earplugs out.


AXIL builds both electronic and passive hearing protection for the construction and industrial roles where these types of problems show up most.

## Common Questions About OSHA Hearing Conservation


What is a hearing conservation program?


A hearing conservation program is the set of noise, hearing and recordkeeping duties OSHA requires under 29 CFR 1910.95(c).


What triggers a hearing conservation program?


Any employee exposure at or above an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA triggers the program.


What are the 5 required elements of a hearing conservation program?


The five commonly listed elements are monitoring, audiometric testing, hearing protectors, training and recordkeeping, though 1910.95 also requires notification, attenuation evaluation and access.


How often is audiometric testing required by OSHA?


OSHA requires a baseline within 6 months of first exposure, then at least one audiogram a year.


Who has to pay for hearing tests and hearing protectors?


The employer pays for both under 1910.95(g)(2) and (i)(1).


What is a standard threshold shift?


A standard threshold shift is an average 10 dB change from baseline at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear.


Is every standard threshold shift recordable on the OSHA 300 log?


No. Under 1904.10, the STS must be work-related and the ear's hearing level must average 25 dB or more.


How long do you have to keep hearing conservation records?


Under 1910.95(m)(3), you keep noise exposure records for 2 years and audiograms for the length of employment. 1910.1020 can require longer retention for some records.


Does OSHA require a written hearing conservation program?


1910.95 doesn't explicitly require a written program, but written procedures are the clearest way to show your program is continuing and effective.


## Where to Start With Your Hearing Conservation Program


Start with a noise survey and a list of every employee working at or above 85 dBA TWA. Those measurements decide who in your workplace gets tested, trained, and protected.


Within 6 months, book a baseline audiogram for everyone on that list, and issue at least three types of hearing protectors checked against your measured TWAs for your employees.


Then set a yearly routine: annual audiograms and training in the same month, every STS reviewed within 21 days, and new monitoring whenever you change equipment or schedules. A routine like that gives your crews a better chance of keeping their hearing for a full career.


Read[1910.95](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.95) and OSHA's hearing conservation program page for the full requirements, and confirm your obligations with a safety professional. Then explore[AXIL's construction and industrial hearing protection](https://goaxil.com/collections/industrial-construction-work) , download the[ANSI test reports](https://goaxil.com/pages/axil-certifications) for your attenuation evaluation, or[contact our team about employer and bulk orders](https://goaxil.com/pages/contact-us) .
